To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a diet with 10% linoleic acid, 1% α-linolenic acid, and a ratio of 10:1, is more effective than a diet with 4% linoleic and 1% α- linolenic and a 4:1 ratio in preventing obesity, bone deterioration, and insulin resistance, in a mouse model of obesity.
the dietary ratio of linoleic to α-linolenic acid (LA/ALA) was not associated with adiposity, insulin sensitivity, or bone mineral density (BMD).
the ratio of dietary linoleic to α-linolenic acid from 10 to >4 by changing only the former did not prevent adiposity or bone deterioration in obese mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of dietary fatty acids on the health of obese mice.
the effects of dietary fat on adipose tissue and bone mass in the obese mouse.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the current study does not show any evidence that the dietary ratio of LA to ALA is a key determinant of adiposity or bone health, and the results are not supportive of any recommendation for a lower LA to ALA dietary ratio in the general population.
the ratio of linoleic to linolenic acid is not a major factor in the development of adiposity and osteoporosis, but that the total amount of linoleic acid is.
a diet containing 10:1 linoleic to α-linolenic acid ratio (LA:ALA), which is the current recommendation, is not necessary to prevent adiposity or bone deterioration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the balance of linoleic acid (18:2n-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (18:n-3) in the diet is important.

the ratio of dietary n-6/n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) should be reduced from 10 to about 4 to prevent adiposity and bone loss in obese mice, and that this is achieved by reducing the dietary n-6 PUFA content.
we found that a low linoleic acid diet, with no change in α-linolenic acid content, did not prevent obesity or bone loss in obese mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ratio of dietary linoleic to α-linolenic acid (LA/ALA) is not the primary factor that drives obesity and bone deterioration in mice.
we have shown that the ratio of linoleic to α-linolenic acid in a high-fat diet has no influence on body weight or bone mass.
the ratio of linoleic to alpha-linolenic acid in the diet is not a major driver of obesity or bone loss in mice.
